## Before you begin

Work individually, with nearby discussion if useful. Predict before each
comparison. No R or GLM experience is required. You may run the supplied code or
read the figures and result sheet; both routes answer the same questions.

Use the prepared browser R environment. If access fails, open this HTML and
[the result sheet](results.html) locally and answer the same questions.
There is one core exercise today. Demonstrations and optional extensions are labelled.
No installation, independent Stan programming or homework is required.

```{r setup}
library(tidyverse)
library(posterior)
library(bayesplot)
library(patchwork)
library(here)
source(here("R/functions.R"))
source(here("R/course_data.R"))

```

# Core exercise: which mother-tree estimates will move?

| | |
|---|---|
| **Purpose** | Explain information sharing using each mother tree's data and the model's assumptions. |
| **Computation** | Supplied partial-pooling fit plus exact Beta updating for the two comparison models. No new Stan inference. |
| **Data** | Eight mother trees of one species. Simulated, and different from the Day 2 quadrats. |

This example leaves out the density predictor so that we can focus on differences
among mother trees. The binomial survival model is shared with Days 1 and 2.
Mother trees and species are different kinds of groups.

## 1. Predict before seeing the fitted results

```{r core-trees}
trees <- make_tree_data()
trees |> select(tree, n, suv) |> mutate(observed_proportion=suv/n)
```

Choose two trees whose estimates you expect to change when they share information.
Write their letters and your reasons. Consider both seedling count and the observed
survival proportion.

## 2. Compare three ways of estimating survival

- **Complete pooling** assumes one shared survival probability.
- **Separate estimates** give each mother tree an independent probability.
- **Partial pooling** gives trees their own probabilities and estimates a shared distribution.

```{r core-comparison}
fit <- course_fit("day3_trees")
fit$source
comparison <- mother_comparison(fit, seed=20261024)
plot_mother_comparison(comparison)
plot_mother_truth(comparison,trees)
```

Purple open points show separate estimates; orange filled points show partial
pooling. The grey vertical line shows the complete-pooling posterior mean,
and the grey ribbon shows its 95% credible interval. Coloured bars are also
95% credible intervals. Rows are ordered by the separate posterior means, and
`n` is the seedling count. Separate and partial intervals are offset vertically
within each tree to keep them distinct. The grey line is a comparison reference,
not the exact target of hierarchical shrinkage.

The second plot compares estimates (y) with the generating probabilities
(x). The dashed diagonal marks equality with the truth. Vertical connections
show movement from Separate to Partial pooling. Tree H (n = 50) changes only slightly,
towards its generating probability of 0.29. Not every tree moves
closer to the truth; in real data, the truth is unknown.

The complete and separate models use the Day 1 flat Beta(1,1) prior on each probability. The partial model uses
Normal group effects on the logit scale, with their centre and SD estimated from
all trees. Thus the prior specifications also differ across these comparisons.

## 3. Interpret the movement

Did your predictions agree with the figures? Explain one tree's change in words.
Would information sharing have the same strength if the data supported large
differences among mother trees? Give a reason.

::: {.content-visible when-meta="solutions"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution and instructor notes

```{r solution-movement, echo=FALSE}
movement <- comparison |> select(tree,n,model,mean) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from=model,values_from=mean) |>
  mutate(change=Partial-Separate) |> arrange(desc(abs(change)))
```

The largest movement in this data set is tree `r movement$tree[1]`, with
`r movement$n[1]` seedlings. Its separate posterior mean is
`r round(movement$Separate[1],2)` and its partial-pooling mean is
`r round(movement$Partial[1],2)`. Ask participants to connect the movement to both
sample size and position relative to the inferred group distribution.

Less information within a group often gives the shared distribution more influence.
Greater inferred between-group variation generally weakens sharing. It does not
move every estimate by a fixed amount or guarantee improvement for every tree.
The target is an inferred distribution on the logit scale, not mechanically the
pooled observed proportion. The comparison also changes the prior formulation.

The true rates are known only because the data are simulated. If revealing them,
use `trees$p_true`. Similar true rates make complete pooling competitive here.
This does not make exact equality a justified assumption for all ecological data.

:::
:::

# Instructor demonstrations

## Shared information as a hierarchical prior

$$
s_j \sim \operatorname{Binomial}(n_j,p_j), \qquad
\operatorname{logit}(p_j) \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma).
$$

Here $j$ indexes mother trees and $\sigma$ is a **standard deviation on the logit
scale**. The supplied `stan/logistic.stan` uses $\mu\sim\mathcal{N}(0,5)$ and
$\sigma\sim\operatorname{HalfNormal}(0,1)$. All Normal second arguments are SDs.

```{r demo-group-spread}
plot_group_spread()
```

The centre is fixed in this illustration. Only the group SD changes. These are
hypothetical probabilities, not posterior estimates for our eight trees.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Completed Stan model

```{r demo-stan, echo=FALSE, results="asis"}
cat("```stan\n",paste(readLines(here("stan/logistic.stan")),collapse="\n"),"\n```\n",sep="")
```

:::

## Computation and ecological checking

```{r demo-diagnostics}
course_diagnostics(fit)
bayesplot::mcmc_trace(fit$draws, pars=c("mu","sigma"))
plot_mother_check(fit)
```

Do the sampler diagnostics agree? Does the model reproduce the observed counts
by mother tree? Is sharing information among these trees ecologically plausible?
A good answer considers all three questions.

## Species differences in CNDD

```{r demo-cndd-species}
plot_cndd_species()
plot_cndd_abundance()
```

These are conceptual simulations from the example in `main.qmd`, not fitted
research results. The individual-level question is survival versus conspecific
density. The group-level question is whether density coefficients vary with
species abundance. The full research analysis is an instructor explanation.
A negative coefficient means declining survival on the probability scale.
More negative logit coefficients do not imply a fixed probability drop at every baseline.

## Another research example: allometry and wood density

The individual-level relationship is height versus DBH. The group-level question
is whether species' allometric exponents vary with wood density. The observation
model changes from binomial survival to Normal log height. Information sharing
among groups is the common structure.

```{r demo-wood-density}
plot_wood_density()
```

This figure uses the existing saved fit to simulated tree data. It illustrates
interpretation, not an empirical conclusion about wood density in a real forest.
No additional participant analysis is required.

# Optional extension: a new mother tree

What can we predict about a ninth mother tree before counting its seedlings?
Keep the model and fitted data fixed. Add variation among mother trees for each draw.

```{r optional-new-tree}
set.seed(20261026)
draws <- fit$draws
p_new <- plogis(rnorm(nrow(draws), draws$mu, draws$sigma))
course_interval(p_new)
```

Does this describe a survival probability or a future number of survivors?

::: {.content-visible when-meta="solutions"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution and instructor notes

It describes the survival probability of a new mother tree under the inferred
group distribution. It includes uncertainty about the group parameters and
variation among mother trees. Predicting a survivor count would also require
specifying a seedling count and generating binomial survival.

:::
:::

# Connection to your research

Name a grouping in your data and one quantity that may differ among groups.
What would justify sharing information? Which predicted pattern would you compare
with observations before reporting the result?
